Probability for ML

Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty. It gives every possible outcome a number between 0 and 1 and supplies rules for combining those numbers. Machine learning uses it to describe noisy data, to say how confident a prediction is, and to update that confidence when new evidence arrives.

1Overview

Why it matters

A classifier that answers "spam, 0.93" is making a probability statement, and what you are allowed to do with that 0.93 follows from the rules in this lesson. Whether to block a payment, send a patient for a second test, rank a comment above another or believe a week of improved metrics are all questions about reading a probability correctly.

The typical failures are quiet. A detector's 90 % hit rate is read as "90 % of alerts are real", when for a rare event most alerts are false. Probabilities of related events are multiplied as if the events had nothing to do with each other. A raw model score is fed into a cost calculation as though it were a measured frequency. A count that drifts by ordinary chance is reported as a change. Nothing crashes in any of these cases; the numbers are simply wrong. Anyone who trains, evaluates or consumes a model needs this vocabulary, because loss functions, classification metrics, naive Bayes, logistic regression and the sampling step of a language model are all written in it.

Before you start

  • What Is Machine Learning?Beginner

What you will be able to do

  • Describe an uncertain quantity as a random variable and read its distribution, discrete or continuous.
  • Compute the expectation, variance and standard deviation of a small discrete distribution by hand.
  • Choose between the Bernoulli, binomial and normal distributions for a quantity and state each one's mean and variance.
  • Calculate conditional probabilities from a table of counts and test whether two events are independent.
  • Apply Bayes' theorem to turn P(evidence given class) into P(class given evidence) and explain the effect of the base rate.
  • Explain why classifiers output probabilities instead of labels and how costs turn a probability into a decision.

Key terms

Random variable
A quantity whose value depends on chance, such as the number of spam emails in the next 20. Written with a capital letter, with a lower-case letter for a particular value.
Distribution
The description of how probability is shared among the values of a random variable. Discrete variables have a probability mass function; continuous ones have a probability density function.
Expectation (mean)
The average of a random variable's values, each weighted by its probability. It is the long-run average over many repetitions.
Variance and standard deviation
Variance is the expected squared distance of a random variable from its mean. The standard deviation is its square root, in the same units as the variable.
Bernoulli distribution
The distribution of a single yes/no outcome that is 1 with probability p and 0 with probability 1 minus p.
Binomial distribution
The distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials that each succeed with the same probability p.
Normal distribution
The bell-shaped distribution for continuous quantities, fixed by its mean and standard deviation. Also called the Gaussian distribution.
Conditional probability
The probability of one event among only those cases where another event happened, written P(A | B) and read as "the probability of A given B".
Independence
Two events are independent when learning that one happened does not change the probability of the other, so their joint probability is the product of the two.
Bayes' theorem
The rule that turns P(evidence | hypothesis) into P(hypothesis | evidence) by weighing it with the prior, the probability of the hypothesis before the evidence was seen.

2Explanation

Introduction

A weather app says "40 percent chance of rain". A spam filter marks a message "spam, 0.93". Both are probability statements, and you already read them the right way: neither claims to know what will happen, and both tell you how strongly to lean. A probability is a number between 0 (cannot happen) and 1 (certain) attached to an event, which is a precisely stated outcome. The precision matters. The US National Weather Service defines (opens in a new tab) its figure as the probability that the forecast point receives at least 0.01 inch of rain, not as the share of the area or of the day that will be wet.

The simplest way to get a probability is to count. Suppose 1,000 old emails have been labelled by hand, and for each one we also record whether it contains the word "free".

Divide by 1,000 to read the table as probabilities. 200 of the emails are spam, so P(spam)=0.20P(\text{spam}) = 0.20P(spam)=0.20. 120 are spam and contain "free", so P(spam and free)=0.12P(\text{spam and free}) = 0.12P(spam and free)=0.12. Now look only at the 160 emails that contain "free": 120 of them are spam, so among those emails the probability of spam is 120/160=0.75120/160 = 0.75120/160=0.75. That last number is a conditional probability. Learning that the word is present moved the estimate from 0.20 to 0.75, and that movement is the whole reason the word is useful to a spam filter.

Three rules hold for every probability in this lesson:

  • Each probability lies between 0 and 1.
  • The probabilities of all the outcomes that can happen add up to 1. The four inner cells of the table give 0.12+0.08+0.04+0.76=10.12 + 0.08 + 0.04 + 0.76 = 10.12+0.08+0.04+0.76=1.
  • The probability that an event does not happen is 1 minus the probability that it does.

Machine learning leans on these ideas in three places. Data are noisy, so a model describes them with a distribution instead of a single value. A classifier's output is a conditional probability, an estimate of P(label∣features)P(\text{label} \mid \text{features})P(label∣features). And training usually means choosing the parameters that make the observed data most probable, which is where the loss in logistic regression comes from.

This lesson covers random variables and the three distributions you will meet first (Bernoulli, binomial and normal), expectation and variance, conditional probability, independence and Bayes' theorem, and finally why models output probabilities and how a probability becomes a decision. It builds on what machine learning is and prepares for statistics for ML, which is about estimating these quantities from samples.

How it works

Random variables and distributions

A random variable is a quantity whose value depends on chance. By convention it gets a capital letter and a particular value gets the lower-case letter, so X=xX = xX=x is the event "X came out as x". In the email table, SSS (1 if spam, 0 if not) and FFF (1 if the email contains "free") are random variables.

A distribution says how the probability is shared among the values.

  • A discrete variable takes separate values, such as a count or a class. Its distribution is a probability mass function (PMF), P(X=x)P(X = x)P(X=x), and the masses add up to 1. Flip three fair coins (opens in a new tab) and let YYY be the number of heads: the masses for 0, 1, 2 and 3 heads are 1/81/81/8, 3/83/83/8, 3/83/83/8 and 1/81/81/8.
  • A continuous variable, such as a duration or a sensor reading, can take any value in a range. Its distribution is a probability density function (PDF) f(x)f(x)f(x). Probability is the area under the curve between two values, so the total area is 1 and any single exact value has probability 0.

Expectation and variance

The expectation, or mean, is the average of the values, each weighted by its probability:

E[X]=∑xx P(X=x)E[X] = \sum_x x \, P(X = x)E[X]=x∑​xP(X=x)

For three coins, E[Y]=0⋅18+1⋅38+2⋅38+3⋅18=1.5E[Y] = 0 \cdot \tfrac18 + 1 \cdot \tfrac38 + 2 \cdot \tfrac38 + 3 \cdot \tfrac18 = 1.5E[Y]=0⋅81​+1⋅83​+2⋅83​+3⋅81​=1.5. No single trial gives 1.5 heads. The expectation is the long-run average over many repetitions. For a continuous variable the sum becomes an integral over the density, and the rules below stay the same.

The variance measures spread: the expected squared distance from the mean μ=E[X]\mu = E[X]μ=E[X].

Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−(E[X])2\mathrm{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2] = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2Var(X)=E[(X−μ)2]=E[X2]−(E[X])2

Here E[Y2]=0+38+128+98=3E[Y^2] = 0 + \tfrac38 + \tfrac{12}{8} + \tfrac98 = 3E[Y2]=0+83​+812​+89​=3, so Var(Y)=3−1.52=0.75\mathrm{Var}(Y) = 3 - 1.5^2 = 0.75Var(Y)=3−1.52=0.75. The standard deviation is the square root, 0.75=0.87\sqrt{0.75} = 0.870.75​=0.87 heads. It is easier to read than the variance because it is in the same units as YYY.

Two rules do most of the work later:

  • Expectations always add: E[aX+b]=aE[X]+bE[aX + b] = aE[X] + bE[aX+b]=aE[X]+b and E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y]E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y]E[X+Y]=E[X]+E[Y], whether or not XXX and YYY are related.
  • Variances add only for independent variables: Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y)\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y)Var(X+Y)=Var(X)+Var(Y). Scaling squares the factor: Var(aX+b)=a2 Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(aX+b)=a2Var(X).

Bernoulli and binomial: yes/no outcomes and their counts

A Bernoulli variable has two values: 1 ("success") with probability ppp and 0 with probability 1−p1 - p1−p. Every binary label is one: spam or not, clicked or not, churned or not. The formulas above give E[X]=pE[X] = pE[X]=p and Var(X)=p(1−p)\mathrm{Var}(X) = p(1 - p)Var(X)=p(1−p), which is largest at p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5 and zero when the outcome is certain.

Add up nnn independent Bernoulli trials that share the same ppp and the total KKK, the number of successes, is a binomial variable:

P(K=k)=(nk)pk(1−p)n−k,E[K]=np,Var(K)=np(1−p)P(K = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1 - p)^{n - k}, \qquad E[K] = np, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(K) = np(1 - p)P(K=k)=(kn​)pk(1−p)n−k,E[K]=np,Var(K)=np(1−p)

(nk)\binom{n}{k}(kn​) counts the ways to choose which kkk of the nnn trials succeed. The mean and variance are the Bernoulli values added nnn times, by the two rules above. Three fair coins are the case n=3n = 3n=3, p=0.5p = 0.5p=0.5: mean 1.5 and variance 0.75, as computed by hand.

python
from math import comb

def binomial_pmf(k, n, p):
    return comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)

print(round(binomial_pmf(2, 5, 0.6), 4))   # 0.2304

The normal distribution

The normal (Gaussian) distribution is the bell curve for continuous quantities. It has two parameters, the mean μ\muμ (where the centre is) and the standard deviation σ\sigmaσ (how wide it is):

f(x)=1σ2πexp⁡ ⁣(−(x−μ)22σ2)f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)f(x)=σ2π​1​exp(−2σ2(x−μ)2​)

Any normal variable can be put on one common scale by standardising: z=(x−μ)/σz = (x - \mu)/\sigmaz=(x−μ)/σ counts standard deviations from the mean. About 68.3 % of the probability lies within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95.4 % within 2 and 99.7 % within 3.

The normal turns up so often because a sum of many independent small effects is approximately normal, largely regardless of how each effect is distributed. A binomial count is such a sum, so for large nnn it is close to a normal with μ=np\mu = npμ=np and σ=np(1−p)\sigma = \sqrt{np(1 - p)}σ=np(1−p)​:

Python's standard library includes the normal distribution as statistics.NormalDist (opens in a new tab), whose cdf(x) method returns P(X≤x)P(X \le x)P(X≤x). The probability of a range is the difference of two such values:

python
from statistics import NormalDist

heights = NormalDist(mu=170, sigma=10)                   # centimetres, illustrative
print(round(heights.cdf(180) - heights.cdf(160), 3))     # 0.683, within one sigma of the mean

Conditional probability and independence

The conditional probability of AAA given BBB restricts attention to the cases where BBB happened:

P(A∣B)=P(A and B)P(B)P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \text{ and } B)}{P(B)}P(A∣B)=P(B)P(A and B)​

In the email table, P(spam∣free)=0.12/0.16=0.75P(\text{spam} \mid \text{free}) = 0.12 / 0.16 = 0.75P(spam∣free)=0.12/0.16=0.75. The order matters: P(free∣spam)=0.12/0.20=0.60P(\text{free} \mid \text{spam}) = 0.12 / 0.20 = 0.60P(free∣spam)=0.12/0.20=0.60 answers a different question. Rearranged, the definition gives the product rule P(A and B)=P(A∣B) P(B)P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)P(A and B)=P(A∣B)P(B).

Two events are independent when knowing one does not change the probability of the other: P(A∣B)=P(A)P(A \mid B) = P(A)P(A∣B)=P(A), or equivalently P(A and B)=P(A) P(B)P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A)\,P(B)P(A and B)=P(A)P(B). Spam and "free" are not independent, because 0.20×0.16=0.0320.20 \times 0.16 = 0.0320.20×0.16=0.032 and the table says 0.12. Dependence between a feature and the label is what makes the feature useful. A feature that is independent of the label says nothing about it.

Independence is usually an assumption, not an observed fact, and it sits under many formulas. The binomial assumes independent trials, and naive Bayes assumes the features are independent of each other once the class is known, which is called conditional independence.

Bayes' theorem

Data often give P(evidence∣class)P(\text{evidence} \mid \text{class})P(evidence∣class) while the decision needs P(class∣evidence)P(\text{class} \mid \text{evidence})P(class∣evidence). Writing the product rule both ways round and dividing gives Bayes' theorem:

P(H∣E)=P(E∣H) P(H)P(E),P(E)=P(E∣H) P(H)+P(E∣not H) P(not H)P(H \mid E) = \frac{P(E \mid H)\,P(H)}{P(E)}, \qquad P(E) = P(E \mid H)\,P(H) + P(E \mid \text{not } H)\,P(\text{not } H)P(H∣E)=P(E)P(E∣H)P(H)​,P(E)=P(E∣H)P(H)+P(E∣not H)P(not H)

P(H)P(H)P(H) is the prior, the probability of the hypothesis before the evidence (the base rate). P(E∣H)P(E \mid H)P(E∣H) is the likelihood, P(H∣E)P(H \mid E)P(H∣E) is the posterior, and the denominator adds up every way the evidence can arise. The prior counts as much as the likelihood: the same evidence gives a very different posterior when the hypothesis is rare, as the worked example shows.

Why models output probabilities

A classifier estimates a conditional probability, P(y∣x)P(y \mid x)P(y∣x): for this input, how likely is each label? Put differently, it predicts the parameter ppp of a Bernoulli variable for every row. Logistic regression does so by passing a weighted sum of the features through the sigmoid function (opens in a new tab), which maps any number into the range 0 to 1. A language model does the same over many classes: it outputs a probability for every possible next token, and sampling parameters reshape that distribution.

A probability is more useful than a bare label for four reasons.

  1. Decisions depend on costs. scikit-learn's guide separates (opens in a new tab) the statistical step (estimate the probability) from the decision step (act on it). predict cuts at 0.5, which is right only when both kinds of error cost the same. If acting wrongly costs cFPc_{FP}cFP​ and failing to act costs cFNc_{FN}cFN​, the expected cost of acting is (1−p) cFP(1 - p)\,c_{FP}(1−p)cFP​ and of not acting is p cFNp\,c_{FN}pcFN​, so acting is cheaper when p>cFP/(cFP+cFN)p > c_{FP} / (c_{FP} + c_{FN})p>cFP​/(cFP​+cFN​).
  2. Evidence can be combined. Probabilities can be multiplied, averaged or updated with a new prior using the rules above. Labels cannot.
  3. Claims can be checked. A model is well calibrated (opens in a new tab) if, among the cases it scores near 0.8, about 80 % turn out positive. The binomial distribution says how far from 80 % the count may drift by chance.
  4. Training needs them. Fitting by maximum likelihood means choosing the parameters that give the observed labels high probability, which leads to the log loss minimised by gradient descent.

A number between 0 and 1 is not automatically a probability. Some models, naive Bayes and support vector machines among them, produce scores that are systematically too extreme or too timid, so check calibration before using a score in an expected-cost calculation.

Worked example: One word in a spam filter: from a table of counts to a posterior, then to a count you can check

The 1,000 labelled emails from the introduction are invented so that the arithmetic stays simple. S=1S = 1S=1 means spam and F=1F = 1F=1 means the email contains "free".

Step 1: probabilities from counts

QuantityCalculationValue
P(S=1)P(S{=}1)P(S=1)200 / 10000.20
P(F=1)P(F{=}1)P(F=1)160 / 10000.16
P(S=1,F=1)P(S{=}1, F{=}1)P(S=1,F=1)120 / 10000.12
P(F=1∣S=1)P(F{=}1 \mid S{=}1)P(F=1∣S=1)120 / 2000.60
P(F=1∣S=0)P(F{=}1 \mid S{=}0)P(F=1∣S=0)40 / 8000.05

Independence would need P(S=1,F=1)=0.20×0.16=0.032P(S{=}1, F{=}1) = 0.20 \times 0.16 = 0.032P(S=1,F=1)=0.20×0.16=0.032. The table gives 0.12, almost four times as much, so the word and the label are strongly dependent.

Step 2: Bayes' theorem

A filter sees the word and needs P(S=1∣F=1)P(S{=}1 \mid F{=}1)P(S=1∣F=1):

P(S=1∣F=1)=0.60×0.200.60×0.20+0.05×0.80=0.120.16=0.75P(S{=}1 \mid F{=}1) = \frac{0.60 \times 0.20}{0.60 \times 0.20 + 0.05 \times 0.80} = \frac{0.12}{0.16} = 0.75P(S=1∣F=1)=0.60×0.20+0.05×0.800.60×0.20​=0.160.12​=0.75

This matches counting directly in the table, 120/160120/160120/160, as it must.

Step 3: change the base rate

Move the same filter to a mailbox where only 2 % of mail is spam. The word behaves as before (0.60 and 0.05), but the prior is now 0.02:

0.60×0.020.60×0.02+0.05×0.98=0.0120.061=0.197\frac{0.60 \times 0.02}{0.60 \times 0.02 + 0.05 \times 0.98} = \frac{0.012}{0.061} = 0.1970.60×0.02+0.05×0.980.60×0.02​=0.0610.012​=0.197

The same evidence now gives 0.20 instead of 0.75. With a prior of 0.50 it gives 0.92.

Step 4: one flagged email is a Bernoulli variable

Back in the first mailbox, let X=1X = 1X=1 if an email containing "free" is spam. XXX is Bernoulli with p=0.75p = 0.75p=0.75, so E[X]=0.75E[X] = 0.75E[X]=0.75 and Var(X)=0.75×0.25=0.1875\mathrm{Var}(X) = 0.75 \times 0.25 = 0.1875Var(X)=0.75×0.25=0.1875.

Step 5: twenty flagged emails are a binomial count

Let KKK be the number of spam emails among the next 20 that contain "free", assuming they are independent of each other. Then KKK is binomial with n=20n = 20n=20 and p=0.75p = 0.75p=0.75:

  • E[K]=20×0.75=15E[K] = 20 \times 0.75 = 15E[K]=20×0.75=15 and Var(K)=20×0.75×0.25=3.75\mathrm{Var}(K) = 20 \times 0.75 \times 0.25 = 3.75Var(K)=20×0.75×0.25=3.75, so the standard deviation is 3.75=1.94\sqrt{3.75} = 1.943.75​=1.94.
  • P(K=15)=(2015) 0.7515 0.255=0.2023P(K = 15) = \binom{20}{15}\,0.75^{15}\,0.25^{5} = 0.2023P(K=15)=(1520​)0.75150.255=0.2023. Even the most likely count happens only one time in five.
  • P(K≤12)=0.1018P(K \le 12) = 0.1018P(K≤12)=0.1018, found by adding the PMF from 0 to 12.

Step 6: the normal approximation

Approximate KKK by a normal with μ=15\mu = 15μ=15 and σ=1.94\sigma = 1.94σ=1.94. Counts are whole numbers, so "at most 12" becomes "below 12.5" on the continuous scale: z=(12.5−15)/1.94=−1.29z = (12.5 - 15)/1.94 = -1.29z=(12.5−15)/1.94=−1.29 and P(Z≤−1.29)=0.098P(Z \le -1.29) = 0.098P(Z≤−1.29)=0.098, against the exact 0.102.

Step 7: check everything in Python

The script uses only the standard library and runs on Python 3.8 or later.

python
import random
from math import comb, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist, mean

counts = {("spam", "free"): 120, ("spam", "other"): 80,
          ("ham", "free"): 40, ("ham", "other"): 760}
total = sum(counts.values())
n_spam = counts["spam", "free"] + counts["spam", "other"]
n_free = counts["spam", "free"] + counts["ham", "free"]
p_spam, p_free, p_both = n_spam / total, n_free / total, counts["spam", "free"] / total
like_spam = counts["spam", "free"] / n_spam            # P(free | spam)
like_ham = counts["ham", "free"] / (total - n_spam)    # P(free | not spam)
print(f"P(spam)={p_spam:.2f} P(free)={p_free:.2f} P(both)={p_both:.2f} product={p_spam * p_free:.3f}")
print(f"P(free|spam)={like_spam:.2f} P(free|not spam)={like_ham:.2f}")

def posterior(prior):
    evidence = like_spam * prior + like_ham * (1 - prior)
    return like_spam * prior / evidence

print("posterior for priors 0.20, 0.02, 0.50:", [round(posterior(q), 4) for q in (0.20, 0.02, 0.50)])

n, p = 20, 0.75
pmf = [comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p) ** (n - k) for k in range(n + 1)]
mu, sigma = n * p, sqrt(n * p * (1 - p))
print(f"mean={mu} sd={sigma:.3f} P(K=15)={pmf[15]:.4f} P(K<=12)={sum(pmf[:13]):.4f}")
print(f"normal approximation of P(K<=12): {NormalDist(mu, sigma).cdf(12.5):.4f}")

random.seed(7)
batches = [sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n)) for _ in range(100_000)]
print(f"simulated: mean={mean(batches):.3f} P(K<=12)={mean(k <= 12 for k in batches):.4f}")
text
P(spam)=0.20 P(free)=0.16 P(both)=0.12 product=0.032
P(free|spam)=0.60 P(free|not spam)=0.05
posterior for priors 0.20, 0.02, 0.50: [0.75, 0.1967, 0.9231]
mean=15.0 sd=1.936 P(K=15)=0.2023 P(K<=12)=0.1018
normal approximation of P(K<=12): 0.0984
simulated: mean=14.998 P(K<=12)=0.1024

What the result means

  • The 0.75 from Step 2 is what a classifier would output for this one feature. It is a conditional probability, and it is valid only for a mailbox with the 20 % base rate it was computed from.
  • A probability of 0.75 does not promise 15 spam emails in every 20. Counts from 13 to 17 cover about 81 % of batches, and 12 or fewer turns up in one batch in ten.
  • That spread is what a calibration check relies on. Only a count far outside the expected range is evidence that the 0.75 is wrong.

Edge cases and limitations

A probability density can be greater than 1
A normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 0.1 has a density of 3.99 at its centre. That is not a probability. For a continuous variable only areas under the curve are probabilities, and any single exact value has probability 0. When a library returns a pdf value, use it to compare how plausible two values are, and use the cdf when you need the probability of a range.
A zero count becomes a zero probability and vetoes everything else
If a word never appeared in the spam you trained on, counting gives P(word | spam) = 0. Multiply that into a product and the whole product is 0, however much other evidence points to spam. The cure is to keep estimates away from 0 and 1, for example by adding 1 to every count (Laplace smoothing). Paul Graham's filter limits every word probability to the range 0.01 to 0.99 for the same reason.
Products of many probabilities underflow to zero
Multiplying 200 factors of 0.01 gives 10 to the power −400, which is smaller than the smallest number a 64-bit float can hold, so the computed result is exactly 0.0. Add logarithms instead of multiplying probabilities. The sum of 200 copies of ln 0.01 is −921.03, an ordinary number, and comparing sums of logs gives the same ranking as comparing the products.
The normal approximation fails for rare events and small samples
With n = 20 and p = 0.02 the exact binomial probability of zero successes is 0.668. The matching normal curve, with mean 0.4 and standard deviation 0.63, gives 0.563 and puts 7.5 % of its area on counts below zero, which cannot occur. The approximation needs both np and n(1 − p) to be comfortably large; a common rule of thumb asks for at least 10 of each. Below that, sum the binomial formula directly.
Independence can appear or disappear when you condition
Two features can be dependent across all emails yet close to independent within the spam class, or independent overall and dependent within a class. Naive Bayes needs the within-class version. Check it on the rows of one class at a time: compare how often two features occur together with the product of their separate frequencies.

When to use it, and when something simpler is enough

Use it when

  • You must act on a prediction and the two kinds of error cost different amounts. Use the predicted probability with a threshold derived from those costs, not the default 0.5 label.
  • You need to know whether a rate or count differs from a claim by more than chance. Model the count as binomial and compare the gap with its standard deviation.
  • A detector's reliability was measured one way round, as a hit rate and a false alarm rate, and you need the probability the other way round. Apply Bayes' theorem with the base rate.
  • A quantity is the sum or average of many independent small contributions, such as measurement noise or a mean over many rows. Describe it with a normal distribution.

Think twice when

  • Observations influence one another, such as votes cast after seeing the current score or many rows from one user. Binomial and product formulas then understate the uncertainty.
  • The data are strongly skewed or heavy-tailed, such as latencies or payment amounts. Summarise them with percentiles, not a normal mean and standard deviation.
  • You have no defensible base rate for the population the system will run on. A single posterior hides that gap, so report the result for a range of priors.

A simpler alternative. Count natural frequencies. Imagine 100,000 cases, split them by the base rate, apply the hit rate and the false alarm rate to each group and read the answer off as a ratio of counts. Or simulate: draw random outcomes in a loop and count how often the event happens. Both agree with the formulas and are harder to get wrong. They stop being enough when there are many pieces of evidence to combine, when values are continuous, or when you need a small tail probability that a simulation would rarely hit.

Key takeaways

  • A random variable is an uncertain number, and its distribution says how probability is shared among its values, as masses that sum to 1 for discrete variables and as area under a density for continuous ones.
  • Expectation is the probability-weighted average and variance is the expected squared distance from it. Expectations always add, while variances add only for independent variables.
  • A yes/no outcome is Bernoulli with mean p and variance p(1 − p). The number of successes in n independent trials is binomial with mean np and variance np(1 − p), and for large n it is close to normal.
  • P(A given B) and P(B given A) are different quantities. Bayes' theorem converts one into the other only with the base rate, which is why detectors of rare events produce mostly false alarms.
  • Independence is an assumption to check, because multiplying probabilities or adding variances is valid only when one event tells you nothing about the other.
  • A classifier outputs an estimate of P(label given features) so that a threshold chosen from the costs of each error can turn it into a decision, and the estimate deserves that use only if it is calibrated.

Sources for this explanation: [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9], [10], [15]

3Real-world applications

5 documented uses of Probability for ML. Each one names the real system, the problem it solves and its tradeoff, with links to the sources.

  1. Bayesian spam filtering: Paul Graham's filter and SpamAssassin's Bayes classifier
  2. FDA antibody test tables: the same test gives a different answer at each prevalence
  3. Reddit's confidence sort: ranking comments by a lower bound on an upvote probability
  4. TrueSkill on Xbox Live: a player's skill held as a normal distribution
  5. Stripe Radar: a fraud probability, a threshold and a break-even calculation

Example 1 of 5

Bayesian spam filtering: Paul Graham's filter and SpamAssassin's Bayes classifier

Paul Graham; Apache SpamAssassinDocumented in an engineering article

Paul Graham's 2002 essay "A Plan for Spam" describes the statistical filter he built for his own mail, including its formulas. The Apache SpamAssassin documentation describes the "naive-Bayesian-style" classifier built into that open-source mail filter and points readers to the same essay. [17][18][19][12]

The problem

A mail filter must decide, for every incoming message, how likely it is to be spam given the words in it, while almost never discarding a legitimate message. Hand-written rules of the form "contains this phrase, add two points" are easy for spammers to dodge, and the points have no clear meaning, so nobody can say how many of them should add up to "spam". The filter also has to fit each user's own mail, because a word that signals spam for one person is routine for another.

Where this topic fits

Training is counting. The number of times each token appears in a corpus of spam and in a corpus of legitimate mail estimates P(token∣spam)P(\text{token} \mid \text{spam})P(token∣spam) and P(token∣not spam)P(\text{token} \mid \text{not spam})P(token∣not spam). At delivery time Bayes' theorem turns those likelihoods into P(spam∣tokens)P(\text{spam} \mid \text{tokens})P(spam∣tokens), treating the tokens as independent once the class is known. The resulting probability is compared with a threshold in Graham's filter, and in SpamAssassin it drives the BAYES rules.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Collect two labelled corpora, one of spam and one of legitimate mail (Graham used about 4,000 messages of each), and split every message into tokens.
  2. Count how often each token occurs in each corpus. The two counts, divided by the corpus sizes, estimate how likely the token is in spam and in legitimate mail.
  3. Turn the two rates into a per-token probability that a message containing the token is spam. Graham doubles the legitimate count to lean against false positives, skips tokens seen fewer than five times, and limits the result to between 0.01 and 0.99 so that no single token is decisive.
  4. For a new message, keep the tokens whose probability is furthest from the neutral value 0.5. Graham keeps fifteen. Those are the tokens that carry the most evidence in either direction.
  5. Combine them with Bayes' theorem under the assumption that tokens are independent given the class: the product of the probabilities, divided by that product plus the product of their complements.
  6. Compare the combined probability with a threshold. Graham treats a message as spam above 0.9, a high bar that reflects how much worse it is to lose a real message than to let one spam through.
  7. Keep learning from newly labelled mail. SpamAssassin's classifier stays inactive until it has learned a minimum number of spam and non-spam messages, and it needs both kinds.

Why this approach fits

A probability has a meaning that a point score lacks. A token value of 0.99 says which way the evidence points and how strongly, and Bayes' theorem says how to combine tokens, so the weights are not left to guesswork. Evidence of innocence counts as much as evidence of guilt: a message from a colleague that mentions "free" is rescued by its other words, as "meeting" pulls the example above down from near-certainty to 0.908.

The counts come from the user's own mail, so the likelihoods fit that mailbox. The independence assumption is false, since words co-occur, but it reduces training to counting and still ranks messages well enough to separate the two classes.

Limitation or tradeoff

Correlated tokens are multiplied as if each were separate evidence, which pushes the combined value towards 0 or 1. It should be read as a score for ranking and thresholding, not as a calibrated probability; the scikit-learn documentation gives the same warning about naive Bayes in general.

The method needs a substantial, user-specific corpus of both classes before it is useful, a token never seen in one class would give a likelihood of zero without clamping or smoothing, and spammers respond by misspelling words or padding messages with innocent text. SpamAssassin's documentation also lists a practical cost: a probabilistic verdict is harder to explain to users than a rule.

What the sources document

  • Graham built the filter from one corpus of about 4,000 spam messages and one of about 4,000 non-spam messages, counting the occurrences of each token in each corpus. [17]
  • In the per-token formula the count from good mail is doubled, tokens that occur fewer than five times in total are ignored, probabilities are limited to the range 0.01 to 0.99, and a word never seen before is assigned 0.4. [17]
  • The fifteen tokens furthest from 0.5 are combined by dividing the product of their probabilities by that product plus the product of their complements, and mail scoring above 0.9 is treated as spam. The essay reports missing fewer than 5 per 1,000 spams with 0 false positives. [17]
  • SpamAssassin's configuration documentation calls its built-in classifier "naive-Bayesian-style" and says the Bayes system does not activate until a minimum number of ham and spam messages have been learned, 200 of each by default. [18]
  • The sa-learn documentation recommends training on at least 1,000 spam and 1,000 ham messages if possible, says that training on one type alone has no effect, refers readers to "A Plan for Spam", and lists difficulty of explaining classifications among the disadvantages. [19]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 2 of 5

FDA antibody test tables: the same test gives a different answer at each prevalence

U.S. Food and Drug AdministrationDocumented in official docs

The FDA page "EUA Authorized Serology Test Performance" lists COVID-19 antibody tests that received emergency use authorization, with each test's measured sensitivity and specificity and the predictive values they imply at stated prevalences. Archived CDC guidance on antigen testing applies the same reasoning under the name pretest probability. [20][21]

The problem

Sensitivity and specificity say how a test behaves when the truth is already known: P(positive∣antibodies)P(\text{positive} \mid \text{antibodies})P(positive∣antibodies) and P(negative∣no antibodies)P(\text{negative} \mid \text{no antibodies})P(negative∣no antibodies). A person holding a positive result needs the reverse, P(antibodies∣positive)P(\text{antibodies} \mid \text{positive})P(antibodies∣positive), and that is not a property of the test alone. It also depends on how common antibodies are among the people being tested, so one figure printed on the box cannot answer the question.

Where this topic fits

Bayes' theorem is the conversion step between the validation study and the interpretation of a result. Sensitivity is the likelihood P(positive∣antibodies)P(\text{positive} \mid \text{antibodies})P(positive∣antibodies), one minus specificity is P(positive∣no antibodies)P(\text{positive} \mid \text{no antibodies})P(positive∣no antibodies), prevalence is the prior, and the positive predictive value (PPV) is the posterior. The FDA carries out the calculation for assumed prevalences and publishes the result beside each test.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. A validation study runs the test on samples whose true status is known. For one listed test, 51 of 52 positive samples and 2,000 of 2,008 negative samples were classified correctly.
  2. Those counts give two conditional probabilities: sensitivity 51/52 = 98.1 % and specificity 2000/2008 = 99.6 %. The false positive rate is therefore 8/2008, about 0.4 %.
  3. Choose a prevalence, the prior probability that a tested person has antibodies. The lowest assumption in the FDA table is 5 %.
  4. Apply Bayes' theorem. In 100,000 people at 5 % prevalence, 5,000 have antibodies and about 4,904 of them test positive, while about 378 of the 95,000 without antibodies also test positive. The PPV is 4,904 / (4,904 + 378) = 92.8 %.
  5. Repeat with a lower prior. At 1 % prevalence the same arithmetic gives about 981 true positives against 394 false positives, a PPV near 71 %. This figure is our own extension of the table.
  6. Where one result is not reliable enough, test again with a second test whose errors are unrelated to the first. The first posterior becomes the new prior, and two positives at 1 % prevalence give a probability above 99 %.

Why this approach fits

A validation study can only measure P(result∣truth)P(\text{result} \mid \text{truth})P(result∣truth), because the truth was fixed when the samples were chosen. The clinical question runs the other way, and Bayes' theorem is the only correct bridge between the two. Publishing the PPV at a named prevalence makes the dependence on the base rate visible, instead of leaving readers to assume that a test with 99.6 % specificity is "99.6 % right".

The same structure applies to any detector of a rare condition: fraud alerts, defect inspection and intrusion detection all report a hit rate and a false alarm rate, and all need the base rate before an alert can be interpreted.

Limitation or tradeoff

The posterior is only as good as its inputs. Prevalence among the people actually tested is rarely known precisely, and it changes over time and from place to place. Sensitivity and specificity are themselves estimates from finite samples: 51 out of 52 leaves a wide range of plausible values, which is why the FDA table prints an interval beside each estimate.

The second-test argument multiplies probabilities, so it assumes that the two tests' errors are independent. Two tests that react to the same interfering substance share their false positives, and the combined result is then less certain than the calculation claims.

What the sources document

  • The page states that positive and negative predictive values are calculated using a test's sensitivity, its specificity, and an assumption about the percentage of individuals in the population who have antibodies to SARS-CoV-2, which it calls prevalence. [20]
  • For the Abbott AdviseDx SARS-CoV-2 IgG II (Alinity) test the table lists sensitivity 98.1 % (51/52), specificity 99.6 % (2000/2008), and a PPV estimate of 92.8 % at an assumed prevalence of 5 % and 96.5 % at 10 %. [20]
  • The page says that in low-prevalence populations a single antibody test result is not likely to be accurate enough to decide whether a person has had a prior infection, and that a second test, typically for antibodies to a different viral protein, would generally be needed. [20]
  • The FDA offers a calculator that shows the estimated performance of a single test or of two independent tests, given their performance characteristics and the estimated prevalence. [20]
  • CDC guidance states that positive and negative predictive values of all in vitro diagnostic tests vary with pretest probability, and lists symptoms, exposure and community prevalence as factors that raise or lower it. [21]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 3 of 5

Reddit's confidence sort: ranking comments by a lower bound on an upvote probability

RedditDocumented in an open-source project

Reddit's open-sourced site code, published in the reddit-archive repository and archived in 2017, contains the function behind its "confidence" comment sort. The function's docstring points to Evan Miller's article "How Not To Sort By Average Rating", which gives the reasoning and names Reddit among the sites that adopted the method. [22][23][24][25]

The problem

Rank comments by quality when the only signal is a pile of upvotes and downvotes. Sorting by upvotes minus downvotes favours whatever has been seen by the most people. Sorting by the upvoted fraction puts a comment with a single upvote, 100 % positive, above one with 100 upvotes and 10 downvotes. The ranking has to reward a high share of upvotes and also account for how little a handful of votes proves.

Where this topic fits

Each vote is modelled as a Bernoulli trial with an unknown probability ppp that a reader upvotes the comment. The votes so far are a binomial sample, and the ranking score is the lower end of a confidence interval for ppp, the Wilson score interval, computed with a quantile of the standard normal distribution. The score is recomputed from two counters as votes arrive, so nothing else needs to be stored per comment.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Treat a comment as having a fixed but unknown upvote probability p, and each vote as one Bernoulli observation of it.
  2. After n votes with u upvotes, estimate p by the observed fraction u/n. Because u is binomial, the variance of that fraction is about p(1 − p)/n, so a few votes leave a lot of uncertainty.
  3. Use the normal approximation to the binomial to turn that variance into an interval for p. The width is set by z, a quantile of the standard normal; Reddit's code uses z = 1.2816, the 90th percentile.
  4. Compute the Wilson lower bound. Unlike the simple "fraction minus z standard errors", it stays between 0 and 1 even with one or two votes.
  5. Sort comments by that lower bound. With Reddit's z, a comment with 1 upvote and no downvotes scores 0.38, one with 40 upvotes and 20 downvotes scores 0.59, and one with 10 upvotes and 1 downvote scores 0.74.
  6. As votes accumulate the bound closes in on the observed fraction. At an 80 % upvote share it is 0.51 after 5 votes, 0.72 after 50 and 0.78 after 500.

Why this approach fits

One number combines "how good" (the upvoted fraction) with "how sure" (the number of votes), and it does so with the variance of a binomial proportion instead of an arbitrary penalty for small samples. It needs two counters per comment and a closed formula, so it is cheap to compute on every page view. A new comment with a few positive votes can overtake an older one, but a single upvote cannot put it at the top.

Limitation or tradeoff

The model assumes votes are independent draws with one fixed ppp. Real votes are not: readers see the current score and position before voting, early voters differ from later ones, and coordinated voting produces correlated votes, so the true uncertainty is larger than the interval suggests. Ranking by a lower bound also holds new comments back by design, and with only a handful of votes any interval built on a normal quantile is rough.

The code comment labels z = 1.2816 as "80% confidence". That is the two-sided reading, with 10 % in each tail. Under the model, the true ppp lies above the bound with about 90 % confidence.

What the sources document

  • The file r2/r2/lib/db/_sorts.pyx in the reddit-archive repository defines _confidence(ups, downs). Its docstring calls it the confidence sort and gives the URL of Evan Miller's article. It returns 0 when there are no votes and sets z = 1.281551565545 with the comment "80% confidence". [22]
  • The function sets p to ups divided by the number of votes and returns p + z²/(2n) minus z·sqrt(p(1 − p)/n + z²/(4n²)), all divided by 1 + z²/n. Results for fewer than 400 upvotes and 100 downvotes are precomputed in a lookup table. [22]
  • Miller's article rejects ranking by positive minus negative ratings and by the fraction of positive ratings, and recommends the lower bound of the Wilson score confidence interval for a Bernoulli parameter. It says the method has since caught on at other sites, naming Reddit among them. [23]
  • In the article's formula, p-hat is the observed fraction of positive ratings, n is the total number of ratings and z is a quantile of the standard normal distribution. [23]
  • The NIST handbook recommends the Wilson method for confidence intervals on a proportion, gives the same formula for its limits, and notes that its lower limit cannot be negative. [24]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 4 of 5

TrueSkill on Xbox Live: a player's skill held as a normal distribution

MicrosoftDocumented in official docs

Microsoft Research's TrueSkill project page describes the skill rating system developed for Xbox Live and used for matchmaking and leaderboards in games such as Halo and Gears of War. The accompanying paper by Herbrich, Minka and Graepel presents it as a Bayesian skill rating system. [26][27]

The problem

Match players of similar ability and rank them on a leaderboard, using nothing but game results. A single rating number cannot tell a veteran with hundreds of games from a newcomer who happened to win twice, and games may involve teams or more than two sides. The system has to say how good a player probably is and also how sure it is about that.

Where this topic fits

Skill is treated as an unknown quantity, and the system's belief about it is a normal distribution with mean μ\muμ (the best guess) and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ (the uncertainty). Each game result is evidence. Bayes' theorem turns the prior belief into a posterior with a shifted mean and a smaller σ\sigmaσ, and matchmaking and the leaderboard read from those two numbers.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Give every new player the same prior belief, a normal distribution with mean 25 and standard deviation 8.333. The wide spread says the system knows almost nothing yet.
  2. When a game ends, treat the finishing order as evidence. By Bayes' theorem the new belief is proportional to the probability of that outcome given the players' skills, multiplied by the old belief.
  3. Shift the means: winners move up and losers move down, and a player whose skill is still uncertain moves further than one whose skill is well established.
  4. Shrink the standard deviations, because every game adds information. In the page's eight-player example the winner moves from (25, 8.333) to (36.771, 5.749) and the last-placed player to (13.229, 5.749).
  5. Rank the leaderboard by the conservative estimate, the mean minus three standard deviations. A newcomer therefore starts near 0 and climbs as the uncertainty falls, even if the mean stays put.
  6. Choose opponents whose skill beliefs overlap, so that the predicted chance of a draw is high and the game is likely to be close.

Why this approach fits

Two numbers summarise the whole belief, and for a normal distribution those two numbers are all there is to know, so storing and updating a belief costs almost nothing per player. Keeping σ\sigmaσ separate from μ\muμ lets the system say "not sure yet": it can move newcomers quickly and veterans slowly, and it can build a cautious leaderboard from a low quantile of the belief instead of its mean. Treating each result as evidence in Bayes' theorem also gives a principled answer to how much one game should count.

Limitation or tradeoff

The normal shape is a modelling choice. Real skill drifts over time and depends on the game mode and on teammates, and the exact posterior after a game is not normal, so each update is an approximation; the paper describes inference by approximate message passing. How fast the belief settles depends on how informative a game is. The page's table gives 3 games per player for a 16-player free-for-all but 91 for two teams of eight, because one team result says little about any individual.

The page describes the mean minus three standard deviations as a value the true skill exceeds with a belief of 99 %. For an exactly normal belief the figure is 99.87 %.

What the sources document

  • The page describes TrueSkill as a skill-based ranking system for Xbox Live developed at Microsoft Research. Skill is characterised by two numbers, the average skill μ and the degree of uncertainty σ, and a new player is assigned μ = 25 and σ = 8.333. [26]
  • The page says the system uses Bayes' law: the new skill beliefs are proportional to the probability of the observed game outcome multiplied by the old skill beliefs. In its eight-player example the winner's μ goes from 25 to 36.771, the eighth-placed player's to 13.229, and both σ values fall to 5.749. [26]
  • Players are ranked by the conservative skill estimate μ − k·σ with k = 3, which the page says the player's actual skill exceeds with a belief of 99 %. [26]
  • The page's table of games needed per gamer lists 3 for a 16-player free-for-all, 12 for a two-player game and 91 for two teams of eight players. [26]
  • The paper's abstract presents a Bayesian skill rating system that builds on the Elo approach, tracks uncertainty about player skills, handles draws and any number of competing entities, infers individual skills from team results, and performs inference by approximate message passing on a factor graph. [27]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

Example 5 of 5

Stripe Radar: a fraud probability, a threshold and a break-even calculation

StripeDocumented in official docs

Stripe's guide "A primer on machine learning for fraud detection" explains how its Radar product scores card payments and how a policy turns scores into actions. Stripe's Radar documentation describes the risk score and risk level attached to each payment. [28][29]

The problem

For every payment, decide in real time whether to allow it, block it or send it to a person for review. Blocking a legitimate customer loses a sale. Accepting a fraudulent payment costs the goods plus a chargeback fee. The two errors have very different costs, and those costs differ from one business to the next, so a single fixed rule cannot be right for everyone.

Where this topic fits

The model's job ends with an estimate of P(fraud∣payment features)P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{payment features})P(fraud∣payment features). A separate policy compares that estimate with a threshold. Expected value links the two: the break-even threshold is the probability at which the expected loss from accepting a payment equals the expected profit given up by blocking it.

How it is applied, step by step

  1. Train a classifier on past payments, each described by features and labelled with whether it turned out to be fraudulent.
  2. For a new payment, output a probability for each class, for example 0.65 fraudulent and 0.35 legitimate, instead of a bare label.
  3. Define a policy as a threshold on that probability, such as "block if the probability of fraud is above 0.7". Raising the threshold makes blocks more precise and lets more fraud through.
  4. Work out what each error costs. In Stripe's example a sale of 26 US dollars at an 8 % margin earns 2.08, while a fraudulent sale loses the 23.92 cost of the goods plus a 15 dollar chargeback fee, 38.92 in all.
  5. Find the break-even point. One fraudulent sale wipes out the profit of 18.71 legitimate ones, so blocking pays for itself whenever more than 1 in 19.71 blocked payments, or 5.07 %, is fraudulent.
  6. In the product the model's assessment is exposed as a risk score from 0 to 99 with default cut-offs: 65 and above is elevated risk, and 75 and above is high risk and blocked by default.

Why this approach fits

Separating the probability from the decision lets one model serve businesses with different economics. A low-margin shop and a software seller with almost no cost of goods should cut at different points on the same score. Because the model's output is a probability, the cut-off can be derived from costs with an expectation instead of being tuned by feel, and the trade between precision and recall can be read off as the threshold moves.

Limitation or tradeoff

The expected-value rule is only as good as the calibration of the probability. If payments scored 0.05 are in fact fraudulent 15 % of the time, the "break-even" threshold loses money. Stripe's documentation describes the 0 to 99 risk score as an indication of risk level and does not present it as a percentage probability, so it should not be dropped into the formula as ppp.

Evaluation is also harder than it looks. Labels arrive late, because a dispute can follow a payment by weeks, and a blocked payment never reveals whether it was fraudulent. The guide says production precision-recall curves require counterfactual analysis for that reason. The calculation ignores costs it does not list, such as a wrongly blocked customer who never returns.

What the sources document

  • The guide says machine learning classifiers typically assign probabilities that a sample belongs to each class, and gives the example of a payment assessed as having a 65 % chance of being fraudulent and a 35 % chance of being legitimate. [28]
  • The guide's example policy blocks a payment when the model assigns a probability of fraud of at least 0.7. It defines precision as the fraction of blocked transactions that are actually fraudulent and recall as the fraction of all fraud caught, and says raising the threshold increases precision and decreases recall. [28]
  • In the guide's worked example an average sale of 26 dollars with an 8 % margin gives a profit of 2.08; a fraudulent sale loses 23.92 plus a 15 dollar chargeback fee, 38.92 in total, which equals the profit of 18.71 legitimate sales, so the break-even precision is 1 / (1 + 18.71) = 5.07 %. [28]
  • Stripe's documentation says each payment can include a risk score from 0 to 99, that by default 65 or above indicates elevated risk and 75 or above high risk, that high-risk payments are blocked by default, and that elevated-risk payments are allowed by default and can be reviewed on plans that support it. [29]
  • The documentation says that for a small subset of payments Stripe modifies the reported risk score in order to measure model performance, so that metrics such as false positive rate and recall stay within desirable ranges. [29]

The facts above come from the cited sources. The steps and analysis in this example are our explanation of how they fit together.

4Common mistakes

  1. Reading P(flagged given real) as if it were P(real given flagged).

    Why it causes problems
    For a rare event the two can differ several times over. A rule that catches 90 % of fraud and flags 2 % of legitimate payments sounds as if nine alerts in ten are real; at a 0.5 % fraud rate fewer than one in five is. A team staffed for the first figure drowns in false alarms and starts ignoring them.
    How to recognise it
    A reliability figure is quoted with no base rate beside it, or a sentence slides from "flags 90 % of fraud" to "90 % of flags are fraud". Rebuild the claim as counts in 100,000 cases and see whether it survives.
    How to fix it
    Write the condition explicitly, with what is known on the right of the bar. Apply Bayes' theorem with the base rate of the population the system will run on, and report the probability that a flagged case is real at that base rate.

  2. Using a raw model score as if it were a calibrated probability.

    Why it causes problems
    Expected-cost thresholds, risk estimates and any product of scores are wrong when 0.9 does not mean "right nine times in ten". Naive Bayes pushes scores towards 0 and 1, some other models avoid the extremes, and training on rebalanced data inflates the probability of the rare class.
    How to recognise it
    Group held-out predictions into bins by score and compare each bin's average score with the fraction of positives in it. If the bin around 0.8 holds 60 % positives, the model is overconfident there.
    How to fix it
    Calibrate on held-out data, for example with scikit-learn's CalibratedClassifierCV, or use the score only for ranking and choose the threshold from validation results instead of from a cost formula.

  3. Multiplying probabilities, or adding variances, for events that are not independent.

    Why it causes problems
    Correlated evidence gets counted twice. Two features that say the same thing push a naive Bayes score to the extreme, and many rows from one user make a count vary more than np(1 − p) allows, so ordinary noise passes for a real effect.
    How to recognise it
    Compare how often two events occur together with the product of their separate frequencies. Check whether rows share a user, session, device or time window. Watch for batch-to-batch variance well above the binomial value.
    How to fix it
    Use the product rule with the conditional probability, P(A and B) = P(A | B) P(B). Merge or drop redundant features, and aggregate to the unit that really is independent, such as one row per user, before applying binomial formulas.

  4. Expecting an observed count to equal its expectation and reacting to ordinary variation.

    Why it causes problems
    A filter that is right 75 % of the time still gets 12 or fewer right out of 20 in about one batch in ten. Teams that read every dip as a regression end up fixing things that are not broken, and teams that read every rise as progress ship changes that did nothing.
    How to recognise it
    A conclusion rests on one small batch, or a rate is reported with no standard deviation or interval next to it. Compute the square root of np(1 − p) and see how many of those the gap amounts to.
    How to fix it
    Put a standard deviation or an interval beside every rate. Before reacting, compute how unlikely the observed count is under the claimed probability, and collect more data when it falls within about two standard deviations of the expected value.

  5. Assuming data are normal and applying three-sigma rules without looking at them.

    Why it causes problems
    Latencies, incomes and purchase amounts have long right tails. A limit at the mean plus three standard deviations should be crossed 0.13 % of the time for normal data; skewed data can cross it many times as often, and the matching lower limit can be negative for a quantity that never is.
    How to recognise it
    The histogram is lopsided, the mean sits well above the median, or the mean minus two standard deviations is below the smallest value the quantity can take.
    How to fix it
    Plot the data first. Set thresholds from percentiles, or take logarithms so that the shape is closer to symmetric. Keep the normal distribution for averages of many independent values and for measurement noise.

5Practice

Exercise 1

Decide whether 33 churners out of 50 contradicts a predicted probability of 0.8

CodingBeginnerAbout 35 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

Last quarter a churn model gave a probability of about 0.80 to each of 50 customers. 33 of them actually churned. A colleague says: "66 % is not 80 %, so the model is broken." Decide whether the gap is larger than chance alone would produce. The scenario is invented for practice.

Use Python with only the standard library (math, random, statistics), which is free and runs on any computer or in a free hosted notebook.

  1. Treat one customer as a Bernoulli variable. If the model is right, what are its mean and variance?
  2. Treat the number of churners among the 50 as a binomial variable KKK. Compute E[K]E[K]E[K], Var(K)\mathrm{Var}(K)Var(K) and the standard deviation.
  3. Compute the exact probability P(K≤33)P(K \le 33)P(K≤33) by summing the binomial PMF.
  4. Compute the same probability with the normal approximation, and the z-score of 33.
  5. Simulate 100,000 batches of 50 customers with random.seed(1) and estimate the probability again.
  6. Write a two-sentence conclusion and name one assumption it depends on.

Requirements

  • Use only the Python standard library, with math.comb for the binomial coefficient and statistics.NormalDist for the normal distribution.
  • Compute the exact tail probability by summing the binomial PMF over 0 to 33, not by simulation alone.
  • Apply a continuity correction in the normal approximation by evaluating the cdf at 33.5.
  • Fix the random seed so that the simulated estimate is repeatable.
  • State the conclusion as a probability of the data under the model's claim, and name the independence assumption.

Expected behaviour

The Bernoulli mean is 0.80 and its variance 0.16. The binomial has mean 40, variance 8 and standard deviation 2.83. The exact P(K≤33)P(K \le 33)P(K≤33) is 0.0144, the normal approximation gives 0.0108, and the z-score of 33 is −2.47. The simulation with seed 1 gives 0.0144. A count as low as 33 would occur in about 1.4 % of batches if every one of these customers really had a 0.8 chance of churning, so the result is evidence that the model is overconfident for this group, though one batch is not proof.

Hint 1

The event "at most 33" covers K = 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 33, so the sum has 34 terms.

Hint 2

If the model is right, each of the 50 customers is one Bernoulli trial with p = 0.8, and the batch total is their sum.

Hint 3

A z-score beyond about 2 in size puts an observation in the outer 5 % of a normal distribution.

Show solution
python
import random
from math import comb, sqrt
from statistics import NormalDist, mean

n, p, observed = 50, 0.80, 33

# 1. One customer: Bernoulli(p)
print(f"Bernoulli: mean = {p:.2f}, variance = {p * (1 - p):.2f}")

# 2. Number who churn out of 50: Binomial(n, p)
mu = n * p
variance = n * p * (1 - p)
sd = sqrt(variance)
print(f"Binomial: mean = {mu:.1f}, variance = {variance:.1f}, sd = {sd:.3f}")

# 3. Exact tail probability
def binomial_pmf(k):
    return comb(n, k) * p**k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)

exact = sum(binomial_pmf(k) for k in range(observed + 1))
print(f"exact P(K <= {observed}) = {exact:.4f}")

# 4. Normal approximation with continuity correction, and the z-score of 33
approx = NormalDist(mu, sd).cdf(observed + 0.5)
print(f"normal P(K <= {observed}) = {approx:.4f}, z = {(observed - mu) / sd:.2f}")

# 5. Simulation
random.seed(1)
batches = [sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n)) for _ in range(100_000)]
print(f"simulated P(K <= {observed}) = {mean(k <= observed for k in batches):.4f}")
text
Bernoulli: mean = 0.80, variance = 0.16
Binomial: mean = 40.0, variance = 8.0, sd = 2.828
exact P(K <= 33) = 0.0144
normal P(K <= 33) = 0.0108, z = -2.47
simulated P(K <= 33) = 0.0144

Reasoning. If the model's 0.8 is right, each customer is a Bernoulli trial and the batch total is binomial with n=50n = 50n=50 and p=0.8p = 0.8p=0.8. The expected count is 40, and the standard deviation of 2.83 says that counts between roughly 34 and 46 are unremarkable. 33 is 2.47 standard deviations below the mean, and the exact calculation puts the probability of a count that low at 1.4 %.

The normal approximation (1.1 %) is close but a little too small, because a binomial with p=0.8p = 0.8p=0.8 has a longer tail on the low side than a symmetric bell curve. The simulation agrees with the exact sum, as it should: both compute the same quantity.

Conclusion. A result this low would happen by chance about once in 70 batches, so it is reasonable evidence that the model's probabilities are too high for these customers, and a good reason to check calibration on more data. It is not proof from a single batch.

Assumptions. The calculation treats the customers as independent. If several belong to one company that cancelled all its accounts together, or one event such as a price change affected them all, the true variance is larger than 8 and a count of 33 is less surprising. It also treats every score as exactly 0.80; with a mix of scores the expected count is the sum of the individual probabilities.

Check your answer

  • Is your exact probability 0.0144, from a sum of 34 terms?
  • Do the exact, normal and simulated answers agree to within about 0.005?
  • Is your binomial standard deviation 2.83, and not 8, which is the variance?
  • Did you phrase the conclusion as "if the model were right, a count this low would occur 1.4 % of the time" and not as "the model is 98.6 % likely to be wrong"?

Exercise 2

Work out what a fraud alert is worth at a 0.5 % base rate

AnalysisBeginnerAbout 30 min (estimate)Hypothetical scenario

A payments team is evaluating an alert rule. The figures are invented for practice.

  • 0.5 % of transactions are fraudulent.
  • The rule flags 90 % of fraudulent transactions.
  • The rule also flags 2 % of legitimate transactions.
  • A manual review costs $3 and always catches the fraud if there is one.
  • A fraudulent transaction that is not reviewed costs $120 on average.

Pen and paper are enough; a spreadsheet or Python is optional.

  1. Fill in a two-by-two table of counts for 100,000 transactions: fraud or legitimate, flagged or not.
  2. Compute P(flag)P(\text{flag})P(flag), P(fraud∣flag)P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag})P(fraud∣flag) and P(fraud∣no flag)P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{no flag})P(fraud∣no flag).
  3. Are "flagged" and "fraudulent" independent? Show it with two numbers.
  4. A second rule with the same two rates also flags the transaction. Assuming the two rules are independent once you know whether the transaction is fraudulent, what is the probability of fraud now?
  5. Using expected cost, should a flagged transaction be reviewed? Should an unflagged one? Above what probability of fraud is a review worth its cost?
  6. Among 200 flagged transactions, what are the expected number of frauds and its standard deviation?

Requirements

  • Show the table of counts for 100,000 transactions with all row and column totals.
  • Use Bayes' theorem, or the equivalent ratio of counts, for the probability of fraud given a flag.
  • Justify the independence answer by comparing a joint probability with a product of two probabilities.
  • State the review decision as a comparison between the review cost and the expected loss.
  • Give the mean and the standard deviation for part 6, and say which distribution you used.

Expected behaviour

Of 100,000 transactions, 500 are fraudulent and 450 of those are flagged; 99,500 are legitimate and 1,990 of those are flagged, so 2,440 are flagged in all. P(flag)=0.0244P(\text{flag}) = 0.0244P(flag)=0.0244, P(fraud∣flag)=0.184P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag}) = 0.184P(fraud∣flag)=0.184 and P(fraud∣no flag)=0.0005P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{no flag}) = 0.0005P(fraud∣no flag)=0.0005. The events are far from independent. Two flags raise the probability of fraud to 0.91. A review is worth it above a fraud probability of 0.025, so flagged transactions are reviewed and unflagged ones are not. Among 200 flagged transactions about 37 are fraudulent, with a standard deviation of about 5.5.

Hint 1

Start from the base rate. Split 100,000 into fraudulent and legitimate first, then apply the flag rates to each group separately.

Hint 2

For two rules, the probability that both flag a fraudulent transaction is 0.9 times 0.9, and the probability that both flag a legitimate one is 0.02 times 0.02.

Hint 3

A review costs 3 dollars every time. Skipping it costs 120 dollars only when the transaction is fraudulent, so compare 3 with 120 times the probability of fraud.

Show solution

1. Counts for 100,000 transactions

FlaggedNot flaggedTotal
Fraudulent45050500
Legitimate1,99097,51099,500
Total2,44097,560100,000

The base rate gives the row totals (100,000×0.005=500100{,}000 \times 0.005 = 500100,000×0.005=500). The flag rates then split each row: 500×0.90=450500 \times 0.90 = 450500×0.90=450 and 99,500×0.02=1,99099{,}500 \times 0.02 = 1{,}99099,500×0.02=1,990.

2. Probabilities

  • P(flag)=2,440/100,000=0.0244P(\text{flag}) = 2{,}440 / 100{,}000 = 0.0244P(flag)=2,440/100,000=0.0244
  • P(fraud∣flag)=450/2,440=0.184P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag}) = 450 / 2{,}440 = 0.184P(fraud∣flag)=450/2,440=0.184
  • P(fraud∣no flag)=50/97,560=0.0005P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{no flag}) = 50 / 97{,}560 = 0.0005P(fraud∣no flag)=50/97,560=0.0005

The same middle answer from Bayes' theorem:

P(fraud∣flag)=0.90×0.0050.90×0.005+0.02×0.995=0.00450.0244=0.184P(\text{fraud} \mid \text{flag}) = \frac{0.90 \times 0.005}{0.90 \times 0.005 + 0.02 \times 0.995} = \frac{0.0045}{0.0244} = 0.184P(fraud∣flag)=0.90×0.005+0.02×0.9950.90×0.005​=0.02440.0045​=0.184

The rule catches 90 % of fraud, yet more than four flagged transactions in five are legitimate, because legitimate transactions outnumber fraudulent ones by 199 to 1.

3. Independence

If the events were independent, P(fraud and flag)P(\text{fraud and flag})P(fraud and flag) would equal 0.005×0.0244=0.0001220.005 \times 0.0244 = 0.0001220.005×0.0244=0.000122. The table gives 450/100,000=0.0045450 / 100{,}000 = 0.0045450/100,000=0.0045, about 37 times larger. They are strongly dependent, which is what makes the flag informative: it raises the probability of fraud from 0.005 to 0.184.

4. Two flags

With the rules independent given the class, the likelihoods multiply:

0.902×0.0050.902×0.005+0.022×0.995=0.004050.00405+0.000398=0.91\frac{0.90^2 \times 0.005}{0.90^2 \times 0.005 + 0.02^2 \times 0.995} = \frac{0.00405}{0.00405 + 0.000398} = 0.910.902×0.005+0.022×0.9950.902×0.005​=0.00405+0.0003980.00405​=0.91

Updating in two steps gives the same result: use 0.184 as the prior for the second flag. The answer depends on the independence assumption. If both rules react to the same signal, such as a new device, the second flag adds little and 0.91 is too high.

5. Expected cost

A review costs $3 whatever the truth is. Not reviewing costs $120 with probability ppp, an expected loss of 120p120p120p. Reviewing is cheaper when 120p>3120p > 3120p>3, that is when p>3/120=0.025p > 3/120 = 0.025p>3/120=0.025.

  • Flagged: the expected loss is 0.184×120=22.130.184 \times 120 = 22.130.184×120=22.13 dollars against a 3 dollar review, so review.
  • Not flagged: the expected loss is 0.0005×120=0.060.0005 \times 120 = 0.060.0005×120=0.06 dollars against 3 dollars, so do not review.

The threshold is 0.025, nowhere near 0.5. A probability of 0.184 means "probably legitimate" and still justifies acting, because missing a fraud costs 40 times as much as a review.

6. Count among 200 flagged transactions

Each flagged transaction is a Bernoulli trial with p=0.184p = 0.184p=0.184, so the count is binomial with n=200n = 200n=200: mean 200×0.184=36.9200 \times 0.184 = 36.9200×0.184=36.9, variance 200×0.184×0.816=30.1200 \times 0.184 \times 0.816 = 30.1200×0.184×0.816=30.1 and standard deviation 5.5. A batch with anywhere from about 26 to 48 frauds is within two standard deviations and is no reason to think the rule has changed.

Check your answer

  • Do the four inner cells of your table add up to 100,000 and the flagged column to 2,440?
  • Is your probability of fraud given one flag 0.184, and given two flags 0.91?
  • Did you compare 0.0045 with 0.000122 (or 0.184 with 0.005) to show the events are dependent?
  • Is your review threshold 0.025, and can you explain why it is so far below 0.5?
  • Is your standard deviation for part 6 about 5.5, the square root of the variance 30.1?

  • Probability for Computer Scientists (opens in a new tab)

    Chris Piech, Stanford University (CS109 course reader)

    BookBeginnerFreeAbout 10 to 15 hours for Parts 1 and 2 (estimate)

    What it teaches
    A full, free course reader for Stanford's CS109 written for programmers. Parts 1 and 2 cover counting, conditional probability, independence, Bayes' theorem, random variables, the named distributions, expectation and variance with worked examples and Python snippets; later parts reach naive Bayes and logistic regression.
    When to use it
    As the main follow-up to this lesson, when you want each topic derived step by step and want many more worked problems than fit here.

  • Seeing Theory (opens in a new tab)

    Daniel Kunin, Brown University

    InteractiveBeginnerFreeAbout 2 hours (estimate)

    What it teaches
    Interactive visualisations of chance events, expectation, variance, conditional probability, discrete and continuous distributions, the central limit theorem and Bayesian updating. You drag sliders and watch the distributions change.
    When to use it
    When a formula in this lesson does not feel intuitive yet and you would rather see it move than read another derivation.

  • statistics — Mathematical statistics functions (opens in a new tab)

    Python Software Foundation

    DocumentationBeginnerFreeAbout 30 minutes (estimate)

    The reference for statistics.NormalDist (pdf, cdf, inv_cdf, zscore, samples) and for the mean, variance and standard deviation functions, with recipes that include approximating a binomial distribution three ways: by a normal curve, by the exact sum and by simulation.
    When to use it
    When you want to compute the numbers in this lesson without installing anything, or to see the binomial approximation recipe that the worked example is modelled on.

    scikit-learn developers

    What a well-calibrated classifier is, how to read a calibration curve, why naive Bayes, random forests and support vector machines are miscalibrated in different directions, and how CalibratedClassifierCV corrects scores with sigmoid, isotonic or temperature scaling.
    When to use it
    Before you use predict_proba output in a cost calculation or show it to users as a confidence level.
